item.title: Takeda Castle Ruins: The Castle in the Sea of Clouds — Guide
item.description: Takeda Castle is one of Japan’s most photographed ruins, and deservedly so. Built in the 15th century on a narrow ridge 353 metres above the Asago valley and abandoned around 1600, all that survives is its remarkable stonework — tiers of ramparts, bailey walls and gate foundations tracing the whole plan of the castle along the mountaintop. On calm, cold mornings in autumn, mist pools in the valley below and the ruins stand clear above a white sea of cloud, an image that has earned it the nicknames ‘Japan’s Machu Picchu’ and ‘the castle in the sky’.

item.title: Tanabe: Castle Ruins and the Gateway to the Kumano Kodo — Guide
item.description: Tanabe, a port town on Wakayama’s western coast, is best known today as the main gateway to the Kumano Kodo, where most pilgrims begin their journey and where the excellent Kumano Tourism Bureau helps foreign walkers arrange routes and lodging. The town itself rewards a wander: the stone walls and water gate of Tanabe Castle survive near the harbour, Morihei Ueshiba, the founder of aikido, was born here and is remembered at a memorial hall, and after dark the narrow lanes of the Aji-koji district fill with small izakaya serving the day’s catch.

item.title: Azuchi Castle Ruins: Nobunaga's Vanished Golden Tower — Guide
item.description: Azuchi Castle was the wonder of its age: the revolutionary fortress-palace Oda Nobunaga raised above Lake Biwa in 1579, its seven-storey tower gilded and painted inside by the era’s finest artists — and it stood barely three years before burning down in the chaos after Nobunaga’s assassination in 1582. What remains is one of Japan’s most evocative ruins: grand stone stairways climbing through cedar woods past the foundation stones of vanished gates and residences to the tower base, where the view over the lake explains at a glance why Nobunaga chose this hill to rule Japan from.

item.title: Utsunomiya Castle Ruins & City: A Reconstructed Earthwork Park — Guide
item.description: Utsunomiya Castle was once a strategically important stronghold along the old Oshu Kaido road connecting Edo to northern Japan, home to a succession of feudal lords over several centuries. Most of the original structure was dismantled after the Meiji Restoration and the site suffered further damage in WWII bombing, but a modern restoration project has rebuilt sections of the earthwork ramparts, moat and a small viewing tower within what is now a landscaped city park, offering a glimpse of the castle’s former layout alongside walking paths and open green space.

item.title: Morioka Castle Ruins & Iwate Park: City Cherry Blossoms — Guide
item.description: Morioka Castle was one of Tohoku’s great fortresses. Only the stone walls remain, but they are spectacular — rising over the Nakatsu River with Iwate-san volcano framed behind. The surrounding Iwate Park (Morioka Castle Ruins Park) is the city’s finest cherry blossom spot, with over 300 trees. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Morioka, Iwate Hours Park always open Admission Free Time needed About 1 hour Best time Late April (cherry blossoms) What to See Spectacular Edo-era stone walls above the river.
